paragraphs.heading: A cell that changes shape
paragraphs.text: An amoeba is a cell, or a single-celled living thing, that can change its shape. It does this mostly by pushing out and pulling back pseudopods. Amoebae are not one group on the tree of life: amoeba-like cells turn up in every major branch of eukaryotes, including protozoa, fungi, algae and animals. Microbiologists often call anything that moves this way an amoeba or an amoeboid.

paragraphs.heading: No longer one group
paragraphs.text: Older classifications put most amoebae together in a group called Sarcodina, defined by having pseudopods or moving by protoplasmic flow. Studies comparing molecules later showed that the members of Sarcodina do not share a single common descent. So amoeboid organisms are no longer grouped together.

paragraphs.heading: How pseudopods work
paragraphs.text: Amoebae have no cell wall, which leaves them free to move. A pseudopod is a bulge of cytoplasm, pushed out against the cell's outer membrane by actin microfilaments acting together. The look of the pseudopods helps tell groups apart. Amoeba itself has blunt, rounded, tube-like ones; Euglypha and Gromia have thin threads; foraminifera spread fine branches that join into nets; and radiolaria and heliozoa have stiff needles braced inside by bundles of microtubules.

paragraphs.heading: Shells and water pumps
paragraphs.text: Some free-living amoebae are testate, living inside a hard shell of calcium, silica, chitin, or stuck-together sand grains and diatom frustules; others are naked. Fresh water holds fewer dissolved substances, such as salt, than the fluid inside the cell, so water keeps moving in by osmosis. Most freshwater amoebae handle this with a contractile vacuole, a compartment that expels the extra water. Without one, the cell would fill up and finally burst. Sea-dwelling amoebae usually lack it, since their insides are in balance with the water around them.

paragraphs.heading: How an amoeba eats
paragraphs.text: Amoebae eat different things. Some hunt bacteria and other protists, while others eat dead organic matter. Usually an amoeba feeds by phagocytosis: it stretches pseudopods around live prey or a scrap of food and engulfs it. It has no mouth, and no fixed spot on the cell where this happens. Some also take in dissolved nutrients by pinocytosis, drawing them in through small vesicles formed from the cell membrane.

paragraphs.heading: From tiny to giant
paragraphs.text: Amoebae vary hugely in size. Massisteria voersi, a marine amoeboid, is only 2.3 to 3 micrometres across, within the size range of many bacteria. Deep-sea xenophyophores build shells up to 20 cm wide. Most amoebae in ponds, ditches and lakes are microscopic, but giant amoebae such as Pelomyxa palustris and Chaos carolinense can be seen with the naked eye.

paragraphs.heading: Signs of sex
paragraphs.text: Recent evidence suggests that several amoebozoan lineages go through meiosis. Acanthamoeba carries versions of genes that sexual eukaryotes use in meiosis, which hints that it may be able to reproduce sexually. The slime mould Dictyostelium discoideum, a so-called social amoeba, can mate and reproduce sexually, meiosis included, when food runs short.
